newsitem.title: USA: Florida sugar tax defeated but fight not over.
newsitem.headline: Florida sugar tax defeated but fight not over.

text.p: The fight to force Florida sugar growers to pay more toward the cost of cleaning up the Everglades is not over despite the defeat of a penny-a-pound sugar tax, tax advocates said Wednesday.

The constitutional amendment, which would have forced farmers to pay an estimated $900 million in the next 25 years, lost 54-46 percent in a statewide ballot Tuesday following the most expensive referendum campaign in Florida history.

But two companion amendments, enshrining in the state constitution the concept of "making the polluter pay" and establishing a trust fund for Everglades restoration, passed easily and will form the basis of a legislative campaign to force farmers to clean up their pollution, tax advocates said.

The heated campaign over the penny-a-pound tax was the culmination of years of debate between environmentalists and sugar growers over pollution of the once-pristine Everglades, a giant marsh that is home to endangered species and the prime source of drinking water for millions of Floridians.
Environmentalists claim water tainted by sugar plantation fertilizers has damaged the slow-moving "river of grass" by spurring the growth of plants which crowd out native species.

Mary Barley, chairwoman of the pro-tax group Save Our Everglades, called the election "bittersweet" because of the tax failure, but said the vote served notice to lawmakers that sugar farmers must pay for Everglades cleanup.
"We're still in play," she said Wednesday. "I think this is a clear mandate to our elected officials to make the polluter pay and to clean up the Everglades."

Barley said her side would urge a reexamination of the 1994 Everglades Forever Act -- in which growers agreed to pay up to $322 million toward a $1.5 billion Everglades cleanup project -- with an eye to making "Big Sugar" pay more.
"We're going to start talking about the plan and how much it is really going to cost. Making the polluter pay means we can reevaluate how much they are paying," she said.
At last report, the two sides had spent nearly $36 million on the campaign, with about $24 million spent by the sugar companies to defeat the tax.

"The money and the organization prevailed," said Tim Lenz, a political science professor at Florida Atlantic University. "They (sugar growers) controlled the terms of the debate" by convincing voters they would have to pay the tax.
The tax failure tossed the issue of Everglades pollution back into the legislative arena, but with the added weight of public sentiment to making the polluter pay, said Lenz.
"They (farmers) dodged a bullet here," he said. "But this issue will not go away. The legislative process pays attention to the numbers."
